definition:
The Bible's teaching on love has two movements that cannot be pulled apart. The first is God's own love: the settled goodwill and faithful commitment by which God chooses, rescues, keeps, and delights in his people and gives himself for the world. The second is the love God commands in return, which Jesus summed up in two sentences drawn from the law of Moses: love the LORD your God with your whole self, and love your neighbor as yourself (Mark 12:29-31, quoting Deuteronomy 6:4-5 and Leviticus 19:18). The New Testament ties the two together so tightly that one cannot be had without the other: “We love because He first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Biblical love is not first a feeling, though it involves the affections deeply. It is loyalty and self-giving that act for another's good, and Scripture measures it finally by the cross: “By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us” (1 John 3:16). This study traces that love from the law to the letters of John; the character of God, the atonement, and the care of the poor have their own studies.

The Hebrew vocabulary centers on the verb ʾāhab (‘to love’) and its noun ʾahăbâ. It covers the whole range of human attachment: a parent for a child (Genesis 22:2), a husband for a wife (Genesis 29:20), friend for friend (1 Samuel 18:1), and the covenant love God commands for himself and the neighbor. Alongside it stands ḥesed, one of the richest words in the Old Testament, which the BSB renders ‘loving devotion’ and older versions ‘steadfast love’ or ‘lovingkindness’. Ḥesed is loyal love that keeps faith within a relationship, especially when the other party has no claim left. The word raḥămîm, usually ‘compassion’ or ‘mercy’, describes tender pity, and it belongs to a word family that includes the ordinary word for ‘womb’, though the connection is one of family resemblance and should not be pressed into every use. In Greek the New Testament chiefly uses agapaō and its noun agapē. The noun was rare in Greek before the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament made from about the third century BC) adopted the verb for ʾāhab, and the New Testament made it the main word for both God's love and Christian love. It also uses phileō (‘to love as a friend’, ‘to be fond of’) and its family, including philadelphia, ‘love of fellow believers’. Erōs, the Greek word for desire, never appears in the New Testament. The words themselves do not carry theology by their roots; agapē means what it means because of what the writers fill it with, and above all because of the cross.
ot:
Love in the Old Testament begins with God's initiative, not Israel's. The first time the Bible uses ʾāhab it is of Abraham's love for Isaac (Genesis 22:2), in the very chapter where that love is tested, and the patriarchal stories are frank about loves that bless and loves that divide (Jacob's favoritism for Rachel and Joseph sets a household at war). But the love that drives the story is God's. Deuteronomy insists that Israel's election was not a reward: “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples” (Deuteronomy 7:7), but “because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers” (Deuteronomy 7:8). God's love has no cause outside itself. When God names himself to Moses after the golden calf, he is the one “abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations” (Exodus 34:6-7), a confession the psalms and prophets repeat more than any other description of God. His love is not soft; the same passage says he will not leave the guilty unpunished. But the covenant rests on ḥesed that outlasts Israel's failures.

The command to love answers that prior love. The Shema, the confession Israel came to recite every morning and evening, joins God's oneness to undivided love: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). In Hebrew the heart is the center of thought and will, not only feeling, and the soul is the whole living self, so the command claims the whole person. Love for God in Deuteronomy is covenant loyalty expressed in obedience (Deuteronomy 10:12-13; 11:1), in the language ancient treaties used for a vassal's allegiance to a great king, and yet it is also personal and inward. Deuteronomy knows that Israel cannot produce this love on its own and promises that God will do it: “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live” (Deuteronomy 30:6).

Love of neighbor is just as old. Leviticus 19, the chapter that begins with the call to be holy because God is holy, forbids hatred and revenge and commands, “love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:18). In context the neighbor is first a fellow Israelite, but the same chapter extends the command to the resident foreigner: “love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:34). Deuteronomy grounds the same duty in God's character: he “loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing. So you also must love the foreigner” (Deuteronomy 10:18-19). Love in the law is concrete. It returns an enemy's stray ox and helps his fallen donkey (Exodus 23:4-5), leaves the edges of the field for the poor, and pays the day laborer before sunset. Proverbs adds that an enemy who is hungry should be fed (Proverbs 25:21), a line Paul later quotes (Romans 12:20). Jewish interpreters noticed the weight of Leviticus 19:18: the Sifra, an early rabbinic commentary on Leviticus, records Rabbi Akiva calling it a great principle of the Torah, and his colleague Ben Azzai answering that Genesis 5:1, the book of the generations of humanity made in God's likeness, is greater still, since it reaches every human being.

The prophets give God's love its most daring language. Hosea is told to take back his unfaithful wife and “Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods” (Hosea 3:1), and God speaks of Israel as a son he taught to walk: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son” (Hosea 11:1). When judgment is deserved, God's heart recoils: “How could I give you up, O Ephraim?” (Hosea 11:8). Jeremiah hears, “I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with loving devotion” (Jeremiah 31:3), and Isaiah compares God's love to a mother's and finds even that too small (Isaiah 49:15). Zephaniah pictures God rejoicing over his people with singing (Zephaniah 3:17). Micah sums up what God asks as justice, loving ḥesed, and humble walking with God (Micah 6:8). The Song of Songs celebrates human love between man and woman as a flame no flood can put out (Song of Solomon 8:6-7), and Ruth's loyalty to Naomi shows ḥesed lived by a foreign widow. The psalms return again and again to one refrain: “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good. His loving devotion endures forever” (Psalm 136:1).
nt:
Jesus did not invent the double commandment; he chose it. When a scribe asked which commandment was most important, he answered with the Shema and Leviticus 19:18 and said, “No other commandment is greater than these” (Mark 12:31). Matthew adds that “All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments” (Matthew 22:40), and in Luke a lawyer gives the same summary himself (Luke 10:27). Jesus' distinctive move comes next. Asked “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29), he tells of a Samaritan, a member of a people many Judeans despised, who stops for a beaten stranger when a priest and a Levite pass by. The story turns the question around: the issue is not whom I am obliged to love but whether I will become a neighbor to whoever lies in the road. In the Sermon on the Mount he goes further: “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be sons of your Father in heaven” (Matthew 5:44-45). The reason is God's own conduct. He sends sun and rain on the evil and the good, and Luke's version says, “He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked” (Luke 6:35). Love that only returns love is ordinary; love of the enemy is the family likeness of God's children.

The Gospel of John grounds love in the life of God himself. Before the world was made the Father loved the Son (John 17:24), and the Son loves his disciples with that same love: “As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love” (John 15:9). On the night before his death, after washing his disciples' feet, Jesus gives “A new commandment” (John 13:34). The command to love was old; what is new is its measure: “As I have loved you, so you also must love one another.” That love is the mark by which the world will recognize his disciples (John 13:35), and its fullest form is death for others: “Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). After the resurrection Jesus asks Peter three times, “do you love Me?” (John 21:15-17), restoring the disciple who had denied him three times, and each answer is met with a charge to feed his sheep. John alternates agapaō and phileō in that exchange. Some interpreters find a deliberate contrast between the two verbs; many others note that John uses them interchangeably elsewhere (the Father loves the Son with agapaō in John 3:35 and with phileō in John 5:20) and read the change as stylistic. Either way, the point of the scene is restoration through love and its outworking in pastoral care.

Paul makes God's love the ground of the whole gospel. “God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). It is love for the undeserving, love for enemies, which is exactly what Jesus had commanded. That love is not only shown but given: “God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5), and nothing in creation “will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). Paul speaks of it personally, of the Son of God “who loved me and gave Himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20). From this love he draws the ethic. Love is the fulfillment of the law, because every command about the neighbor is summed up in Leviticus 19:18 (Romans 13:8-10; Galatians 5:14). Faith works itself out “through love” (Galatians 5:6), love is the first fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), and believers are to “walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us” (Ephesians 5:2). In 1 Corinthians 13, written to a church proud of its spiritual gifts, Paul says that tongues, prophecy, knowledge, and even martyrdom are nothing without love, describes love by what it does and refuses to do (“Love is patient, love is kind”), and ends by ranking it above faith and hope because it alone will never pass away (1 Corinthians 13:13).

The other apostolic writers agree. James calls Leviticus 19:18 “the royal law” and refuses a love that honors the rich and dishonors the poor (James 2:1-9). Peter writes, “Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). The first letter of John gives the Bible's most direct statement: “God is love” (1 John 4:8, 16). John does not reverse the sentence, as if whatever people call love were God; he defines love by what God has done: “love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4:10). From there he draws the test that runs through the whole letter: anyone who claims to love the unseen God while hating the brother he can see is a liar (1 John 4:20), and love that sees a brother in need and closes its heart is no love at all (1 John 3:17). In Revelation the risen Christ warns a church that has kept its doctrine but lost “your first love” (Revelation 2:4). The canon closes with a marriage (Revelation 19 and 21), the love of God for his people brought to its goal.

keyTexts.why: The source of ‘love your neighbor as yourself’, set in a chapter on holiness and paired with the ban on grudges and revenge. Verse 34 extends the same love to the foreigner.
The Shema joins God's oneness to undivided love for him with heart, soul, and strength. Jesus calls it the first and greatest commandment.
God's love for Israel has no cause outside itself: he chose them because he loved them, not because they were many or impressive.
God speaks as a father who taught his son to walk and whose heart recoils from giving him up. The Old Testament's most intimate portrait of God's love under provocation.
Jesus commands love of enemies and grounds it in the Father who sends sun and rain on the evil and the good.
Jesus joins the Shema and Leviticus 19:18 as the two greatest commandments, and the scribe agrees they outrank every offering.
The parable of the good Samaritan turns ‘Who is my neighbor?’ into the question of who proved to be one.
The ‘new commandment’: love one another as Christ has loved us, the mark by which the world will know his disciples.
The Father's love for the Son flows through the Son to the disciples, and its greatest form is laying down one's life for friends.
God proves his love in Christ's death for sinners and pours that love into believers' hearts by the Spirit.
Love of neighbor fulfills the law; every command about the neighbor is summed up in Leviticus 19:18.
Paul's portrait of love, written to a gifted and divided church: without love every gift is nothing, and love outlasts faith and hope.
‘God is love’, defined by the sending of the Son as an atoning sacrifice. Love for God and love for the brother stand or fall together.

history:
The early church was known for its love before it was known for its theology. Christian writers of the second and third centuries describe common funds for widows, orphans, prisoners, and the burial of the poor, and Tertullian's Apology (about 197) reports that pagans remarked on how Christians loved one another. When the emperor Julian (reigned 361 to 363) tried to revive the old religion, he complained in a letter to a pagan priest that the Christians supported not only their own poor but pagan poor as well. Augustine of Hippo gave the Western church its classic theology of love. In On Christian Teaching (begun about 396) he distinguished loving a thing for its own sake from valuing it in relation to something higher, and taught that God alone is to be loved for his own sake and everything else in relation to him. In The City of God (15.22) he defined virtue briefly as the right order of love (ordo amoris): sin is not loving bad things so much as loving good things in the wrong order. His homilies on 1 John (about 407) made love the test of every practice, including discipline in the church.

Medieval theologians built on that foundation. Richard of St Victor (twelfth century) argued in his On the Trinity that perfect love requires another to love and a third to share it, reasoning from love toward the plurality of persons in God. Bernard of Clairvaux, in On Loving God, traced four degrees of love, from loving oneself for one's own sake to loving oneself only for God's sake. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae, II-II, questions 23 to 27) described charity as a kind of friendship with God, the form of all the virtues, and discussed an order of charity by which nearer obligations (family, fellow believers) rightly take priority within a love that excludes no one. Martin Luther, in the Heidelberg Disputation of 1518, set God's love against human love: human love is drawn to what it finds attractive, while God's love creates the goodness it loves. John Wesley taught that the goal of the Christian life in this world is ‘perfect love’, love for God and neighbor filling the heart, in A Plain Account of Christian Perfection (1766). Jonathan Edwards preached sixteen sermons on 1 Corinthians 13 in 1738, later published as Charity and Its Fruits (1852), and Søren Kierkegaard's Works of Love (1847) pressed the command to love the neighbor one actually sees.

The twentieth century argued over whether Christian love is a different kind of love altogether. The Swedish Lutheran Anders Nygren, in Agape and Eros (published in two parts, 1930 and 1936), contrasted self-giving agapē with acquisitive erōs and judged that the church had often mixed them. C. S. Lewis's The Four Loves (1960) described affection, friendship, and erotic love as natural goods that become demons when they make themselves gods and are healed only by charity. Pope Benedict XVI's first encyclical, God Is Love (2005), argued that erōs and agapē belong together in a single reality of love. Gene Outka's Agape: An Ethical Analysis (1972) mapped the debate among Protestant and Catholic ethicists. Throughout, the churches have kept the double commandment at the center of catechesis: the Heidelberg Catechism (1563) states what God's law requires in the words of Jesus' summary, the Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647) gives the same summary as the sum of the Ten Commandments, and Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant teaching alike treat love of God and neighbor as the sum of the moral life. The site's page on God's attributes discusses how God's love relates to his holiness, justice, and impassibility.

differ.view: Agape as a love distinct from desire
differ.body: Christian love is God's own kind of love, unmotivated by the worth of its object and poured out on the undeserving, and it must not be confused with the natural love that seeks its own fulfillment. God loved sinners while they were enemies (Romans 5:8, 10); Jesus commands love that expects nothing back (Luke 6:35). When the church blended agapē with the ancient ideal of erōs, the soul's longing to rise to the beautiful, love for God became a ladder of desire and self-perfection. Defenders in this line, of whom Anders Nygren is the best known, want to keep grace pure: human beings love because God first loved them, not because they climb toward him.

differ.view: Love as desire healed and rightly ordered
differ.body: God made human beings to desire, and the problem is not desire but disordered desire. Scripture speaks freely of longing for God (Psalm 42:1-2; 63:1), and the Song of Songs celebrates erotic love as good. Augustine taught that every love finds its rest only in God, and that the cure for sin is the right ordering of loves, not their suppression. On this view, held with differences by Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, C. S. Lewis, and Benedict XVI, grace does not replace natural love but heals and elevates it, so that a person's desire for joy is fulfilled in loving God and others for God's sake.

differ.view: An order of love with special obligations
differ.body: Love excludes no one, but it is not identical toward everyone. Scripture itself gives priority to those nearest: a person who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8), and believers are to do good to all, especially the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). Augustine and Aquinas taught an order of charity in which family, neighbors, and fellow believers carry nearer claims, because finite creatures can serve only those God places within reach. Defenders say this is not favoritism but faithfulness to one's actual callings, and that it grounds love for the stranger rather than competing with it.

differ.view: Neighbor love as universal and self-giving regard
differ.body: Jesus' answer to ‘Who is my neighbor?’ was a Samaritan helping a stranger, and his command reaches to enemies. Defenders of this emphasis, including Søren Kierkegaard and many modern Christian ethicists, argue that the order of love easily becomes a license to prefer one's own kind, and that the New Testament's pressure runs outward, toward the foreigner, the enemy, and the one who cannot repay (Luke 14:12-14). They grant that duties to family are real, but insist that the neighbor is whoever is in need before me and that equal regard for every person as made in God's image must govern every nearer love.

errors:
The church has rejected any attempt to set a loving God against the God of the Old Testament. Marcion, excommunicated at Rome about 144, taught that the just and wrathful God of Israel was a lesser deity than the loving Father revealed by Jesus, and cut his Bible down to an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul. The church answered that the God who is love in 1 John is the God who named himself ‘abounding in loving devotion’ at Sinai, and that the two great commandments are both quotations from the law of Moses. A related distortion treats love as the opposite of holiness and judgment, so that love means approving whatever a person wants. Scripture's love rejoices in the truth and takes no pleasure in evil (1 Corinthians 13:6), disciplines the children it loves (Hebrews 12:6), and reached its height in a cross that took sin seriously enough to die for it. Love is not measured by what it permits but by what it gives.

Other errors come from the opposite side. Love can be reduced to feeling, so that a person who does not feel warmly believes he cannot love, when Scripture commands love as a matter of the will and action (1 John 3:18). Love can be turned into a way of earning God's favor, when the whole Bible insists that God's love comes first and ours answers it. And love can be preached for God while the neighbor is neglected, a split John calls a lie (1 John 4:20). The church's own history includes cruelty done in God's name to Jews, heretics, and enemies, and the command to love enemies judges that history as it judges every believer. A doctrine of love that never confronts one's own hardness has not yet heard it.
life:
The doctrine begins with receiving, not achieving. Scripture's order is fixed: God loved first, and human love answers. People who have learned to earn affection by performance, or who were rarely loved well, often find it easier to serve God than to believe he delights in them, and the Bible's answer is not a technique but a fact about God: he set his love on his people because he loved them (Deuteronomy 7:7-8), and nothing can separate them from it (Romans 8:39). Prayer, worship, and obedience grow from there. Loving God with heart, soul, mind, and strength means that love reaches thinking, desiring, choosing, and the use of one's body and resources, not only moments of religious feeling.

Love of neighbor is almost always local and specific. It looks like patience with a spouse, time given to a child, a visit to someone in the hospital, honesty in business, and the refusal to hold a grudge. Jesus' parable makes the neighbor whoever lies in the road, which means love is often inconvenient and rarely chosen in advance. The command to love enemies is the hardest test, and the New Testament meets it with concrete first steps: pray for them, do good to them, and do not repay evil for evil (Luke 6:27-28; Romans 12:17-21). None of this is possible by resolve alone; love is the fruit of the Spirit, and the church is where it is learned, practiced, and forgiven when it fails.
questions: Jesus answered ‘Who is my neighbor?’ with a story about a Samaritan. Who are the people you would least like to see as your neighbor, and what would it look like to become a neighbor to them?
1 John 4:10 defines love by what God did rather than by what we feel. How does that change the way you judge whether you love God or another person?
Paul says love fulfills the law (Romans 13:8-10), yet he also calls love the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22). How do command and gift fit together in the Christian life?
